title: Building the customer portal
intro: Now it is time to turn the capstone plan into a working application. You will build the customer portal from the inside out, starting with a walking skeleton and then connecting the Spring Boot backend, PostgreSQL database, and React frontend into one coherent system.
body:
## Start with a walking skeleton

The biggest risk in a capstone is spending days building one layer in isolation and discovering later that the pieces do not fit together. A **walking skeleton** is a very small version of the complete application that works end to end.

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "Walking skeleton first", "caption": "A thin slice through every layer, deployed on day one — then thicken it feature by feature.", "steps": [{"label": "React page", "sub": "one route"}, {"label": "GET /api/health", "sub": "one endpoint"}, {"label": "Flyway V1", "sub": "one table"}, {"label": "CI", "sub": "build + test"}, {"label": "Deploy", "sub": "a public URL"}]}
~~~

For the customer portal, the first walking skeleton could be surprisingly small:

~~~text
React login page
      ↓
POST /api/auth/login
      ↓
Spring Security
      ↓
JWT returned
      ↓
React stores authentication state
      ↓
GET /api/me
      ↓
Customer dashboard
~~~

At this point you do not need beautiful styling, invoices, ticket chat, or every database relationship. You want to prove that the browser can communicate with the backend, authentication works, and the frontend can display authenticated data.

This approach reduces integration risk early. Once the skeleton works, each new feature becomes an incremental extension instead of another unknown integration problem.

## Build the backend around resources

The backend should expose a small, predictable REST API. For this capstone, the initial endpoint set can be:

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose | Authentication |
|---|---|---|---|
| POST | /api/auth/login | Authenticate a user | Public |
| GET | /api/me | Return the current user | Required |
| GET | /api/orders | Return the customer's orders | Required |
| GET | /api/tickets | Return the customer's tickets | Required |
| POST | /api/tickets | Create a ticket | Required |
| GET | /api/tickets/{id}/messages | Return ticket messages | Required |
| POST | /api/tickets/{id}/messages | Add a ticket message | Required |

These endpoints are enough to establish the main customer workflow.

The backend should own the rules about what a user is allowed to access. If customer A requests customer B's order, the server must reject the request even if the frontend never displays a link to that order.

This distinction is important throughout the capstone: **the frontend controls the user experience; the backend controls access to data and operations.**

## Authentication with Spring Security and JWT

The login endpoint accepts credentials and, after successful authentication, returns a signed JWT. JWT means JSON Web Token: a compact token containing claims that the server can verify.

A simplified response could look like:

~~~json
{
  "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9..."
}
~~~

The React application then sends the token with protected requests:

~~~text
Authorization: Bearer <token>
~~~

Spring Security should validate this token before allowing protected controllers to execute.

A typical request flow is:

1. The user submits the login form.
2. React sends credentials to `/api/auth/login`.
3. Spring Security authenticates the credentials.
4. The backend creates a signed JWT.
5. React stores the authentication state according to the application's security design.
6. The API client adds the token to protected requests.
7. Spring Security validates the token.
8. The controller receives the authenticated user context.

Do not put authorization logic only in React. A malicious user can call your API without using your interface at all.

## DTOs keep the API boundary clean

A DTO, or Data Transfer Object, is an object designed specifically for communication across a boundary such as an HTTP API.

Avoid returning JPA entities directly from every controller. An entity represents your persistence model, while a DTO represents what the API should expose.

For example, your internal user entity might contain a password hash, audit information, and relationships. None of those necessarily belong in the `/api/me` response.

A response DTO could be much smaller:

~~~java
public record MeResponse(
    Long id,
    String name,
    String email,
    String role
) {}
~~~

For incoming requests, use validation annotations where appropriate:

~~~java
public record CreateTicketRequest(
    @NotBlank
    @Size(max = 200)
    String title,

    @NotBlank
    @Size(max = 5000)
    String message
) {}
~~~

The controller can then use `@Valid` to trigger validation.

Validation belongs on the backend even when the frontend validates the same fields. Frontend validation gives users fast feedback. Backend validation protects the actual application boundary.

## Create the database with Flyway

The database should be reproducible. Instead of manually creating tables on each machine, use Flyway migrations.

A migration might create the initial users table:

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    email VARCHAR(320) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    role VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL
);
~~~

Later migrations can add orders, invoices, tickets, and messages.

Use sequential migration names such as:

~~~text
V1__create_users.sql
V2__create_orders.sql
V3__create_invoices.sql
V4__create_tickets.sql
V5__create_messages.sql
~~~

The exact naming convention depends on your Flyway configuration, but the principle is consistent: **schema changes should be versioned alongside the application code**.

This makes a new developer's setup much easier. Clone the repository, start PostgreSQL, run the application, and Flyway brings the schema to the expected version.

## Build the React routes around user journeys

The frontend should reflect how the user thinks about the application. A reasonable route structure is:

~~~diagram
{"type": "tree", "title": "Routes follow user journeys", "root": {"label": "/", "children": [{"label": "/login"}, {"label": "/app", "sub": "<RequireAuth>", "highlight": true, "children": [{"label": "/app/orders", "children": [{"label": "/app/orders/:id"}]}, {"label": "/app/tickets", "highlight": true, "children": [{"label": "/app/tickets/new"}, {"label": "/app/tickets/:id"}]}]}, {"label": "/admin", "sub": "role ADMIN"}]}}
~~~

~~~text
/login
/dashboard
/orders
/tickets
/tickets/:id
~~~

The login route is public. The remaining customer routes require authentication.

The dashboard can initially be simple. It might show the user's name, a count of open tickets, recent orders, and links to the main sections.

The orders page displays the customer's orders. The tickets page lists tickets and provides a way to create one. The ticket detail page displays the conversation and allows the customer to send another message.

If you later add administration, use a separate protected area such as `/admin/tickets`. The frontend can hide that route from ordinary customers, but the backend must independently enforce the admin role.

## Create one API client

Do not scatter raw `fetch` calls throughout every component. Create a small API client that handles common behavior in one place.

For example:

~~~ts
async function api(path: string, options: RequestInit = {}) {
  const token = localStorage.getItem('token');

  const response = await fetch(path, {
    ...options,
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
      ...(token ? { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } : {}),
      ...(options.headers ?? {})
    }
  });

  if (response.status === 401) {
    localStorage.removeItem('token');
    window.location.href = '/login';
    throw new Error('Unauthorized');
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error('Request failed');
  }

  return response.json();
}
~~~

This gives your application a single place for authentication headers and common HTTP error handling.

For a production application, carefully consider the security properties of token storage and your overall authentication architecture. The capstone is an opportunity to understand those trade-offs rather than blindly copying a pattern.

## Loading, empty, and error states

A component that only handles the successful response is not finished.

For example, the ticket page can have at least four meaningful states:

~~~text
Loading
   ↓
Success → tickets exist
   ↓
Success → no tickets
   ↓
Error
~~~

The loading state prevents the interface from appearing broken while the request is in progress.

The empty state answers a different question: the request succeeded, but there is currently no data. “No tickets yet” is much more useful than an empty white area.

The error state gives the user a way to understand that something went wrong. Depending on the error, you might provide a retry button.

These states should be designed intentionally for every data-fetching screen.

## Build the ticket workflow incrementally

Tickets are a good example of vertical feature development.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Ticket lifecycle", "nodes": [{"id": "o", "label": "OPEN", "highlight": true}, {"id": "p", "label": "IN_PROGRESS"}, {"id": "w", "label": "WAITING_FOR_CUSTOMER"}, {"id": "c", "label": "CLOSED"}], "edges": [{"from": "o", "to": "p", "label": "admin picks up"}, {"from": "p", "to": "w", "label": "asks a question"}, {"from": "w", "to": "p", "label": "customer replies", "dashed": true}, {"from": "p", "to": "c", "label": "resolved"}]}
~~~

Start with creating a ticket:

~~~text
Ticket form
    ↓
POST /api/tickets
    ↓
Validate request
    ↓
Save Ticket
    ↓
Return Ticket DTO
    ↓
Update React state
~~~

Then implement the list endpoint. After that, implement ticket details and messages.

Do not try to build real-time chat first. A normal request/response conversation is enough for the MVP. Once the basic workflow is reliable, you can consider WebSockets or another real-time mechanism as an enhancement.

This is a recurring engineering principle: **make the simplest useful version work before increasing technical complexity**.

## Test each layer

The capstone should have tests at several levels.

For the backend, unit tests can cover business rules such as ticket status transitions or authorization decisions. Integration tests can verify repositories, database behavior, and Spring components working together.

Controller or API-level tests can verify HTTP status codes, validation responses, and authorization behavior.

For React, component tests can verify that ticket lists render correctly, forms validate input, and user interactions update the interface.

End-to-end tests can verify an important complete journey, for example:

~~~text
Login
  ↓
Open tickets
  ↓
Create ticket
  ↓
Open ticket detail
  ↓
Send message
  ↓
See message in conversation
~~~

Do not attempt to test every implementation detail. Test the behavior that matters to the user and the business rules that would be dangerous to break.

## Run the stack with Docker Compose

Your local development environment should be reproducible. Docker Compose can run PostgreSQL alongside the application services.

A simplified structure might be:

~~~yaml
services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: portal
      POSTGRES_USER: portal
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: portal
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"

  backend:
    build: ./backend
    depends_on:
      - db
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  frontend:
    build: ./frontend
    depends_on:
      - backend
    ports:
      - "5173:5173"
~~~

The exact development setup can differ. What matters is that another developer can understand how to start the environment without manually reproducing undocumented configuration.

Environment variables should contain configuration that changes between environments. Never commit real production passwords or JWT secrets to the repository.

## Deploy before the project feels finished

Deployment should not be the final task on the final evening.

A practical sequence is:

1. Deploy the backend skeleton.
2. Connect it to a managed PostgreSQL database.
3. Configure production environment variables.
4. Deploy the frontend.
5. Configure the production API URL.
6. Configure HTTPS and the custom domain.
7. Run database migrations.
8. Verify health checks.
9. Test the main customer journey.

A deployment that happens early becomes another development environment. Problems with CORS, environment variables, database connectivity, migrations, or routing are much easier to solve before the application contains dozens of features.

## Keep commits understandable

Commit hygiene matters because a capstone is also a demonstration of how you work.

Prefer small commits with a clear purpose:

~~~text
feat(auth): add JWT login endpoint
feat(tickets): create ticket API
feat(tickets): add customer ticket list
feat(frontend): add protected routes
fix(tickets): prevent cross-customer access
 test(api): cover ticket authorization
~~~

Avoid commits such as `stuff`, `changes`, or `final final 2`.

A useful commit should tell another developer what changed. If you discover a bug while implementing a feature, a separate fix commit can make the history easier to understand, especially when the change is independently meaningful.

Commit working increments frequently. Your Git history becomes a lightweight development diary and makes debugging or reverting changes easier.

## A practical build order

A sensible order for the customer portal is:

### 1. Foundation

Create the frontend, backend, PostgreSQL configuration, Docker Compose setup, Flyway, and CI.

### 2. Authentication

Create users, password hashing, login, JWT generation and validation, `/api/me`, and protected React routes.

### 3. Customer data

Implement orders and invoices, then connect the corresponding React screens.

### 4. Tickets

Implement ticket creation and listing, followed by ticket details and messages.

### 5. Administration

Add admin authorization and the ticket management interface.

### 6. Quality

Add validation, tests, error handling, logging, monitoring, and accessibility improvements.

### 7. Production

Deploy, verify migrations, configure HTTPS, test the production environment, and document the setup.

This order deliberately keeps the most important integration paths working throughout the project.

## Common mistakes

### Building the frontend and backend separately

If the frontend is developed for weeks using mocked data, API mismatches can appear very late. Connect a real endpoint as early as possible.

### Returning entities directly

This can accidentally expose internal fields and tightly couples the API contract to the persistence model. DTOs give you a deliberate API boundary.

### Trusting the frontend for authorization

A hidden button is not a security control. Every protected backend operation must verify the authenticated user and required role or ownership.

### Ignoring empty states

No data is a normal state, not necessarily an error. Design it explicitly.

### Adding real-time chat too early

Real-time communication is interesting, but it adds infrastructure and failure modes. First make ordinary ticket messaging reliable.

### Deploying once at the end

Late deployment turns infrastructure problems into deadline problems. Deploy the skeleton early.

### Huge commits

A massive commit containing authentication, tickets, UI redesign, deployment, and database changes is difficult to review and difficult to debug. Prefer coherent increments.

## The complete project

The capstone is intentionally designed so that you can build it yourself rather than simply copy a finished application. Once you understand the architecture, however, comparing your implementation with a complete example can be extremely useful.

The **full sample customer-portal project is available on Patreon**. Use it as a reference after attempting the milestones yourself: compare the project structure, API boundaries, security decisions, tests, Docker setup, and deployment configuration with your own choices.

The goal is not to reproduce someone else's code line by line. The goal is to be able to explain why your implementation works and why you made the architectural decisions you made.

## Definition of a finished feature

Before calling a customer-portal feature complete, ask:

- Does the backend implement the required behavior?
- Are inputs validated?
- Is authorization enforced on the server?
- Is the database change represented by a migration?
- Does the frontend handle loading, empty, success, and error states?
- Are important behaviors tested?
- Does the feature work through the Docker-based local setup?
- Does CI pass?
- Does the production environment work?
- Is the code understandable to another developer?

That checklist is more valuable than simply asking whether the feature “works”. A capstone should demonstrate that you can take a requirement through the entire software development lifecycle: design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance.
takeaways: Build a walking skeleton early so all major layers work together.
Keep authorization on the backend and expose deliberate DTOs.
Use Flyway to make database schema changes reproducible.
Centralize API communication and handle authentication failures consistently.
Design loading, empty, error, and success states as part of the feature.
Deploy early and keep commits small, coherent, and understandable.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a walking skeleton?
options: To create the final production UI before backend development.
To prove that the major application layers can work together end to end.
To replace automated tests with manual testing.
To eliminate the need for database migrations.
quiz.explanation: A walking skeleton is a minimal end-to-end implementation that proves the frontend, backend, authentication, database, and other important layers can communicate.

quiz.question: Why should a customer portal use DTOs instead of always returning JPA entities directly?
options: DTOs make PostgreSQL unnecessary.
DTOs automatically encrypt every API response.
DTOs provide a deliberate API boundary and prevent accidental exposure of internal fields.
DTOs remove the need for Spring Security.
quiz.explanation: DTOs allow the API contract to be designed independently from the persistence model and help prevent internal or sensitive entity fields from being exposed.

quiz.question: What should the backend do when a customer requests another customer's order?
options: Return the order because the frontend should have hidden the link.
Return the order only if the customer knows the order ID.
Ignore the request and continue normally.
Reject the request because the backend must enforce ownership and authorization.
quiz.explanation: The backend is the security boundary. It must verify that the authenticated user is allowed to access the requested resource.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of Flyway migrations?
options: To version and reproduce database schema changes.
To generate React routes.
To store JWT tokens in the browser.
To replace Spring Security.
quiz.explanation: Flyway records database schema changes as versioned migrations so environments can be brought to a known schema state consistently.

quiz.question: Why is it useful to handle loading, empty, and error states separately?
options: Because successful API responses should never be displayed.
Because every request always produces exactly one of those states.
Because they represent different real application conditions that require different user feedback.
Because React cannot render a list without them.
quiz.explanation: Loading means the request is still running, empty means it succeeded but has no data, and error means the operation failed. Treating them separately produces a clearer user experience.

exercise.title: Build an interactive ticket panel
exercise.task:
Define exactly these names: `INITIAL_TICKETS` and `App`.

`INITIAL_TICKETS` must contain the initial tickets exactly as specified: `{ id: 1, title: "Invoice missing", status: "open" }`, `{ id: 2, title: "Change delivery address", status: "closed" }`, and `{ id: 3, title: "Login problem", status: "open" }`.

`App` must render an interactive ticket panel. Add a select with `aria-label="Status filter"` and options `all`, `open`, and `closed`, with `all` selected initially. Add a `ul` with `aria-label="Tickets"`. It must contain one `li` for each visible ticket, with text in the form `<title> (<status>)`. Each open ticket must contain a `button` with the text `Close`; clicking it changes that ticket's status to `closed`. Closed tickets must not have a Close button.

Add a form containing an input with `aria-label="New ticket title"` and a submit button with the text `Create`. Submitting a trimmed title shorter than 5 characters must show a `p` with `role="alert"` and exact text `Title must be at least 5 characters`, without adding a ticket. A valid trimmed title must add a new ticket with the next available numeric ID and status `open`, clear the input, and remove the alert. Add a `p` with `data-testid="open-count"` showing `<n> open`, where `n` is the number of currently open tickets.

Do not call `createRoot` or render `App` yourself. The sandbox renders `App` for the tests.
exercise.hint: Keep the ticket list in React state rather than rendering directly from `INITIAL_TICKETS`. Use one state value for the filter, one for the input, and one for the validation error. When closing a ticket, use `map` to create a new array. When creating a ticket, calculate the next ID from the current tickets and append the new object. The visible list and open count should both be derived from the current state.

tests.name: It renders the initial tickets and open count
It filters tickets by status
It shows Close only for open tickets and closes a ticket
It rejects a short title without adding a ticket
It creates a valid ticket with a trimmed title
It assigns the next numeric id to a new ticket
It removes the validation alert after a successful create
It keeps filtering applied after closing or creating tickets
